unsorted.remarks_to_the_author:
I would like to thank the authors for the detailed responses. Most of my questions have been well answered. The following are additional comments for the updated submission.

In Figure 1c, I believe the deep learning models, including DeepSynergy, MARSY, and DeepDDs, can be pre-trained. As long as they have some trainable parameters, those parameters can be updated using a pre-training dataset like DrugComb and then fine-tuned on datasets D1-D3. I do not see any issues that prevent pre-training them. The results in Figure 3a are model performance for the models trained from scratch. I think it may be because BAITSAO has some pre-trained components like GPT-3.5 so that BAITSAO outperforms other models (which are trained from scratch). Therefore, it is necessary to pre-train all these models (including BAITSAO, DeepSynergy, MARSY, and DeepDDs) on DrugComb and then fine-tune them on D1-D3 to perform a fair comparison.

How did the author compute the PCC between embeddings from DrugBank descriptions and LLM-generated descriptions? The embeddings are vectors and not scalars. How is the PCC of vectors computed?

In Figure 2 (a), the authors should use cosine similarity, instead of using PCC, to measure the similarity between the drug embedding vectors. PCC is used for measuring the correlation between two random (scalar) variables.

I also agree with Reviewer #1 (as in the authors' response) that referring to this approach as a foundational model may be overstated. The proposed method highly relies on GPT 3.5 to generate textual descriptions and embeddings of drugs and cell lines. The accuracy of the descriptions relies on the well known knowledge of the known drugs stored in the GPT models. Although the authors replied that we can use the similarity of a new drug to known drugs to infer its synergy effect with other drugs, it still needs to access the new drug's functions, which are unknown or incomplete in the drug development stage. Due to these limitations to apply the BAITSAO model, it is hard to say it is a foundation model.

(Remarks on code availability)

The code provides a README file with enough instructions for installing and running the application. I am able to install and run the code.

After a thorough review of both the manuscript and the authors' responses to the reviewers' comments, I believe they have put in significant effort and have addressed all the raised concerns convincingly.

(Remarks on code availability)

## REVIEWER COMMENTS

General Response: We are grateful for your valuable feedback. In response, we have modified our descriptions for models to avoid overstatement, performed more ablation tests to demonstrate the advantages of our method, and revised the descriptions of our results and methods for more clarity.

EDITORIAL NOTE: This Reviewer was not able to submit their report; however, they have been replaced by Reviewer #3. They have expressed that the following points were not addressed:

- Comment #1, as the Reviewer believes that BAITSAO may not qualify as a foundation model; its generalisability to potential drugs where minimal information is available remains unclear.

Response: Thank you for your comments. We have revised the description of our methods and avoid overstatement. We will not emphasize this model as a foundation model but as a unified model powered by pre-training and embeddings from large language models, as BAITSAO is capable of performing classificationlevel and regression-level tasks.

Regarding the question of potential drugs with minimal information, we have demonstrated the embedding similarity between the description from DrugBank (only with functional information) and that from LLM. Therefore, we believe that BAITSAO can predict drug synergy reliably with its chemical and functional annotations.  For drugs without such information, predicting synergy effect will be challenging and is worth pursuing in the future, provided information from novel drug combinations for predicting and testing is available. We have elaborated in this in the updated Discussion section (page 17, lines 499-505).

- Comment #2: the Reviewer notes that the architecture of DeepSynergy does not appear to differ significantly from that of BAITSAO, but there is a large performance gap. Please provide further explanation on this observation.

Response: Thank you for your comments. We intend to demonstrate the better performance of BAITSAO versus DeepSynergy from three aspects. First, BAITSAO has a larger parameter size (134M versus 40M by DeepSynergy) and has BatchNorm layers to accelerate convergence speed, so they have different model architectures. According to the scaling law [1], models with larger parameter sizes likely have a stronger generalization ability, which is also demonstrated in Figures 6 (e) and (f). Second, BAITSAO is integrated with advanced training strategies widely used in model pre-training/fine-tuning [2], such as a learning rate scheduler and Adam optimizer, which can help obtain a better model and improve both convergence speed and generalization ability [3]. Finally, BAITASO can perform multi-task learning with an uncertainty-weighting strategy in the pre-training stage, which allows the model to leverage the benefits of different tasks and improve the performances together. We also tested pre-training DeepSynergy but it performed worse than BAITSAO after fine-tuning. Therefore, BAITSAO is different from DeepSynergy from the perspective of model design.

Response: Thank you for your acknowledgment of our effort. Your invaluable feedback is helpful.

In Figure 1c, I believe the deep learning models, including DeepSynergy, MARSY, and DeepDDs, can be pre-trained. As long as they have some trainable parameters, those parameters can be updated using a pre-training dataset like DrugComb and then finetuned on datasets D1-D3. I do not see any issues that prevent pre-training them. The results in Figure 3a are model performance for the models trained from scratch. I think it may be because BAITSAO has some pre-trained components like GPT-3.5 so that BAITSAO outperforms other models (which are trained from scratch). Therefore, it is necessary to pre-train all these models (including BAITSAO, DeepSynergy, MARSY, and DeepDDs) on DrugComb and then fine-tune them on D1-D3 to perform a fair comparison.

Response: Thank you for your comments. We now pre-trained all deep-learningbased models, including MARSY, DeepSynergy, and DeepDDs, for tasks assigned to D1 (regression), D1 (classification), D2 (regression), and D3 (classification). As MARSY is designed for regression-level tasks and DeepDDs is designed for classification-level tasks, we pre-trained these models based on the original tasks and loss functions, which can also be used to explore the potential benefits brought by pre-training these models. According to Extended Data Figure 11, BAITSAO still shows better performance compared to other baselines with either fine-tuning mode or from-scratch mode. Moreover, methods including MARSY and DeepDDs do not benefit from pre-training apparently, and pre-training DeepSynergy with finetuning can only improve the classification performance on one dataset, which does not show strong generalization ability. Therefore, the multi-task pre-training strategy of BAITSAO is unique and contributive, which leads to consistent improvement across different datasets. We have summarized these in the Results section of our revised manuscript (pages 12-13, lines 370-377).

How did the author compute the PCC between embeddings from DrugBank descriptions and LLM-generated descriptions? The embeddings are vectors and not scalars. How is the PCC of vectors computed?

Response: Thank you for your questions. PCC can be used to describe the similarity of word embeddings or sentence embeddings as the average embedding is close to 0 [1], and PCC is easy to compute based on a DataFrame object [2]. Here we select the embeddings of drug A's description from LLMs and embeddings of drug A's description from DrugBank. Since these two embeddings have the same dimension

𝑛𝑛 , we can compute the PCC between these two embeddings. The only difference between PCC and cosine similarity (CS) [3] in this part is whether we need to consider the sample mean or not, but we have replaced PCC with CS in the similarity comparison of this manuscript. We computed the mean absolute error between the CS and PCC results, which is very small (1.3e-4). Please see the details in our responses to the following question.

In Figure 2 (a), the authors should use cosine similarity, instead of using PCC, to measure the similarity between the drug embedding vectors. PCC is used for measuring the correlation between two random (scalar) variables.

Response: Thank you for your suggestion. We have replaced all the similarityrelated analyses computed based on PCC with cosine similarity. Please check the updated Figure 2 and Extended Data Figure 4.
